summary: Gives security guidelines for the Softwire Hubs and Spokes and Mesh solutions. It analyzes vulnerabilities and discusses protections such as authentication, integrity and confidentiality.

plainLanguage.summary: Tunnels carry traffic between sites, and bad actors might try to spy or meddle. This lists the dangers and the locks to use.

questions: why not use group pre-shared keys
what is a rogue softwire concentrator
subtitle: Which attacks threaten softwire tunnels, and which protections, mostly IPsec, an implementation has to provide.

tldr.problem: Softwires carry IPv4 across IPv6 networks and the reverse, often over public networks, so both their control packets and their data packets can be snooped, altered, replayed or flooded.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC analyzes threats for the Hubs and Spokes (L2TPv2) and Mesh (BGP) designs, then requires authentication, integrity and replay protection for control traffic, with IPsec ESP and IKE as the main tools.
tldr.outcome: It gives concrete MUST, SHOULD and MAY levels for both designs and example IPsec policies, but covers tunnel security only, not end-to-end protection.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
The Softwire Working Group standardizes how to connect IPv4 networks across IPv6 networks and IPv6 networks across IPv4 networks. This RFC gives security guidelines for two solution spaces, Hubs and Spokes and Mesh, both described in RFC 4925.

For Hubs and Spokes, L2TPv2 is the phase 1 protocol. If it runs over an unprotected network it MUST be protected by a security protocol such as IPsec (RFC 3193). New implementations SHOULD use IKEv2 for key management. For Mesh, BGP distributes softwire routing information, and BGP's own security is handled in other working groups.

The document talks about the tunnel between the endpoints. If end-to-end security is needed, a security protocol SHOULD be used in the payload packets, and that is out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: Tunnels connect networks that speak different languages. This paper says how to keep those tunnels safe in two different layouts.

sections.title: Hubs and Spokes Deployment Cases
sections.content:
The softwire initiator (SI) sits in the customer network and connects to a softwire concentrator (SC) in the service provider network. The SI may be a CPE device, a router behind it, or a host such as a laptop. The nomadic case, where it moves between networks, SHOULD be supported.

Three cases are considered. In Case 1 the SI reaches the SC of its home provider through the home access network, both under the same administration. In Case 2 the SI reaches its home SC through a visited access network, such as a Wi-Fi hot-spot, that the home provider does not trust. In Case 3 the SI connects to an SC in a visited provider that has a roaming agreement with the home provider.

The SC checks the SI with the help of AAA servers: a home AAA server (AAAh) and, for roaming, a visited AAA server (AAAv).
sections.plainLanguage: A laptop may connect from home, from a cafe to its own company, or to a different company that has a friendship deal with its own. Each trip needs different care.

sections.title: Trust Relationships
sections.content:
In Case 1 the SC and the home AAA server MUST have a trust relationship and their communication MUST be secured. In Case 2 a trust relationship between the SI and the home SC MUST be established, and because the visited network may be public, the SI and SC MUST authenticate each other.

In Case 3 the visited AAA server MUST trust the home AAA server and their communication MUST be secured. When AAA proxies sit between them, the AAA proxy threat model (RFC 2607) SHOULD be considered, because a malicious proxy may attack passively or actively and longer chains are less trustworthy.
sections.plainLanguage: Before you hand your secrets over, you need to know who you are talking to, and the people passing messages along have to be trustworthy too.

sections.title: Threats to Hubs and Spokes Softwires
sections.content:
In Hubs and Spokes, L2TPv2 is used only in a voluntary tunnel model: the SI acts as the L2TP Access Concentrator and PPP endpoint, and always starts the tunnel with a Start-Control-Connection-Request (SCCRQ). L2TPv2 offers an optional CHAP-like tunnel authentication that needs a shared secret and has no key management. PPP authentication gives no per-packet authentication, PPP encryption is weak, and PPP authentication has no scalable key management.

The steps are open to man-in-the-middle, denial-of-service and service-theft attacks. The listed adversary actions are snooping for identities and other confidential information, modifying control and data packets, replaying captured control messages to hijack a tunnel or PPP connection, flooding with bogus signaling to terminate tunnels, and disrupting negotiation to weaken confidentiality or the PPP LCP authentication.

Without prior trust, a node can pretend to be an SC. A rogue SC can blackhole traffic or eavesdrop on all packets to and from the SI. Ingress filtering of inner addresses helps, but it does not fully stop address spoofing, so authentication that binds the legitimate address to the authenticated identity MUST be implemented, for example with IPsec.
sections.plainLanguage: A bad guy might read the mail, change it, copy old letters, flood the pipe, or pretend to be the post office. Just checking addresses is not enough.

sections.title: Required Protections and Authentication
sections.content:
The softwire security protocol MUST protect control messages against eavesdropping and spoofing, protect itself against replay, protect the device identifier from impersonation, bind the authenticated session to the client's device identifier to prevent service theft, and protect disconnect and revocation messages. For control packets, authentication, integrity and replay protection MUST be supported and confidentiality SHOULD be. For data packets, authentication, integrity and replay protection SHOULD be supported and confidentiality MAY be.

User authentication in the control plane MUST be supported. A cleartext PAP password can be stolen. CHAP (RFC 1994) mitigates that but is one-way, so a rogue SC is still possible. EAP-TLS requires mutual authentication and avoids the rogue SC. Mutual authentication MUST be supported. PPP CHAP and L2TPv2 tunnel authentication MUST NOT be used unprotected on a public IP network.

A provider may allow unauthenticated connections, for example when the customer is already authenticated by other means. This MUST be configurable by the SC administrator, and the SC SHOULD use ingress filtering and logging. Such a service cannot offer integrity, replay protection or confidentiality.
sections.plainLanguage: Both sides must prove who they are, and the messages must be sealed so nobody can change or replay them. A plain password sent in the open is a bad idea.

sections.title: Using IPsec to Protect L2TPv2
sections.content:
Softwire-security-compliant implementations MUST implement IPsec ESP in transport mode (RFC 4303) for control and data packets, and IKE (RFC 4306) for authentication, security association negotiation and key management. NAT traversal MUST be supported, including UDP encapsulation of ESP (RFC 3948) and NAT-traversal negotiation in IKE (RFC 3947).

For quick deployment, RFC 3193 MUST be supported, but new implementations and deployments SHOULD use IKEv2 because it is more reliable in replay protection and DoS protection. IKEv2 also supports EAP, which SHOULD be used when both machine and user authentication are needed, such as in the nomadic case.

Pre-shared keys suit only small numbers of SIs and SCs. A scalable key management approach MUST be provided and certificates are preferred where possible. Group pre-shared keys MUST NOT be used, because of their vulnerability to man-in-the-middle attacks.

Other points: an SC implementation SHOULD NOT change its IP address or port in the SCCRP, and if a change is needed it signals this with a StopCCN and a new IKE_SA and CHILD_SA MUST be set up. Since ESP transport mode changes the IP header, the UDP checksum is affected; the 'incremental update of checksum' option of RFC 3948 MUST NOT be used, and the 'do not check' option is a simple approach. IKEv2 and ESP traffic (IP protocol 50, UDP ports 500 and 4500) MUST be allowed to bypass policy.
sections.plainLanguage: IPsec is a locked, tamper-proof envelope. The rules say which envelope to use, how to swap keys, and not to share one key with a whole crowd.

sections.title: Mesh Security Guidelines
sections.content:
In the Mesh solution, Address Family Border Routers (AFBRs) connect access islands across a transit core of a different address family. They use BGP to exchange softwire encapsulation sets and reachability. All AFBRs in the transit core MUST have a trust relationship with each other, and there MUST be a trust relationship between each PE and its CE, although the PE-CE link may be unprotected. The architecture is much like a provider-provisioned VPN, so the threats in RFC 4111 apply.

Data attacks include sniffing, modifying, spoofing or replaying packets, deleting traffic, flooding with unauthenticated data, and traffic analysis of size, timing and addresses. On the control plane, BGP is vulnerable to the threats described in RFC 4272.

Mesh setup MUST support authentication, though the core provider may turn it off. TCP MD5 for BGP (RFC 2385) has key management shortcomings, and IPsec can counter insertion, deletion, modification and man-in-the-middle attacks. For data, the softwire MUST support IPsec tunnels with ESP with null encryption or AH, and ESP with encryption MAY be applied when part of the core is untrusted. Keys MUST be distributed automatically by IKEv2, with a pre-shared key that is the same in all routers (a group key) or public keys. Public keys SHOULD be used if stronger key management is needed. Filters and access control are a necessary addition to cryptography against DoS.
sections.plainLanguage: In the mesh layout, many routers talk to each other. They must trust each other and lock their conversations, and filters at the door keep strangers out.
